title: Chmielnik’s Survivors and the Kielce Pogrom
summary: The return of survivors followed by renewed anti-Jewish violence makes the immediate postwar years essential to understanding the community’s fate.

![Chmielnik, the town to which survivors returned](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/f/f7/Market_Square_in_Chmielnik_%283%29.jpg/1920px-Market_Square_in_Chmielnik_%283%29.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=api&utm_content=thumbnail)

## A return, not a liberation scene

The memorial book’s caption is brief: “The first group of the surviving remnant in Chmielnik, 1945.” It identifies the photograph as a gathering of survivors; it does **not** say they arrived together on a particular day, or that the scene depicts a liberation. The caption is preserved in two records of the same image: [First survivors’ group in Chmielnik]( /communities/chmielnik/records/event_candidate_472cde52807452831b9b2c6c) and [First group of survivors in Chmielnik, 1945](/communities/chmielnik/records/mention_4123cb95fdc6e09b7338628a).

In the seated row, the caption names [Rebeka Sametband](/communities/chmielnik/records/mention_b375122833c8c86274fe3915), [Israelke](/communities/chmielnik/records/mention_b296b5509db15598152de9e2), [Esther Wigadni](/communities/chmielnik/records/mention_bc11875f300cc6c35f9ff602), and [Gitl Shulzinger](/communities/chmielnik/records/mention_9eaec11123eaa7900b690011). Standing are [Shaul Marawitch](/communities/chmielnik/records/mention_9eda1b34ed6d3d0b46ebdd88), [Meir Mali](/communities/chmielnik/records/mention_907facdb5b57a31ff099ec8e), [Mindl Garlitsky](/communities/chmielnik/records/mention_050851d53f1325d7524ce73a), [Tashe Wigadni](/communities/chmielnik/records/mention_40a4481e6c95f184d159efed), and [Israel-Yitzhak Ridelnik](/communities/chmielnik/records/mention_47c856921c74e9f639590a28). These names make the photograph more than a generic image of “survivors”: they return individual Chmielnikers to the story. But the caption supplies no ages, family relationships, wartime routes, or later fates. Those details should not be guessed from the names alone.

The memorial book places this first group in a town whose Jewish community had been destroyed. Its chapter list also includes Yosef Kantor’s “Return to Poland After the War,” alongside the accounts of the pogrom victims. That structure preserves two sharply different experiences of return: the hope, however tentative, of finding survivors and home again, and the renewed danger that followed. The English pages on JewishGen are a translation of *Pinkes Khmielnik*, not independent confirmation of its testimony. ([jewishgen.org](https://www.jewishgen.org/yizkor/chmielnik/chmielnik.html))

## Chmielnik names among the dead in Kielce

The book’s accounts identify four Chmielnik Jews killed in the [Kielce pogrom](/communities/chmielnik/records/event_candidate_879bbc98a971ac145ff2549a) on 4 July 1946. The record naming the date reports four victims but says only three names are legible or clear in the passage; another account also identifies four Chmielnikers, while the supplied OCR is uncertain about the place-name. The spellings vary across the records, so they should not be forced into a single, falsely precise list.

The named victims include [Shmuel Weinberg](/communities/chmielnik/records/mention_8710c734c04e0deb8e5918ff), also rendered in the evidence as Samuel Weinberg, Shmuel Weigberg, or Veinberg; [Moshe Widl Eisenberg](/communities/chmielnik/records/mention_95811c5030564c7e909437ef), whose name also appears as Moshe Yuddel Einberg or Moshe Yudl Eisenberg; [Mendel Mikalowski](/communities/chmielnik/records/mention_440c397dd081446593486b0b); and [Frau Flutga](/communities/chmielnik/records/mention_3e0bc05e6441dccb9e824ae7). The last name is given as “Frau Flutga”—“Mrs. Flutga”—rather than a full personal name. One record describes Mendel as having died in the pogrom; another identifies him as Mikalowski. The sources supplied here do not establish whether “Mendel” and “Mendel Mikalowski” are certainly the same person. The book also preserves a separate account titled “Shmuel Veinberg – A Victim of the Kielcer Pogrom,” by Chaya Rozenblum-Frucht, underscoring how one death could be remembered in an individual family voice as well as in a communal list. The record [Deaths of Chmielnik Jews in the Kielce pogrom](/communities/chmielnik/records/event_candidate_ae2d49a5acce7d54e6c7354a) gives the date as 4 July 1946; the related records call the place “Kelce” or “Kielce,” spellings that point to Kielce but reflect uncertain transcription. ([jewishgen.org](https://www.jewishgen.org/yizkor/chmielnik/chmielnik.html))

The distinction between the book’s accounting and the wider record matters. The memorial-book evidence says four Chmielnik Jews were killed; it does not supply a complete victim register or explain how each person came to be in Kielce. The US Holocaust Memorial Museum’s overview, by contrast, describes the pogrom in the city as a whole: on 4 July, amid a false kidnapping accusation and antisemitic blood-libel rumors, civilians, soldiers, and police killed 42 Jews and wounded 40. It estimates that about 200 Jewish survivors had returned to or settled in Kielce by that summer. That wider account establishes the scale and setting of the massacre, but does not independently verify the Chmielnik victims’ names. ([encyclopedia.ushmm.org](https://encyclopedia.ushmm.org/content/en/article/the-kielce-pogrom-a-blood-libel-massacre-of-holocaust-survivors))

## A regional catastrophe, and what remains unresolved

The setting was a postwar region where survival did not guarantee safety. Historian David Engel’s study, available through Yad Vashem, places Kielce within a broader pattern of anti-Jewish violence in Poland from 1944 to 1946 and discusses attacks on Jews returning to towns after the war. Its regional frame helps explain why the return pictured in Chmielnik and the killings in Kielce belong in the same history: for survivors, coming back could mean searching for family, shelter, or a recognizable home while facing the possibility of further violence. Engel’s study is not a second account of the Chmielnik photograph or proof of the four names; it adds historical context. ([collections.yadvashem.org](https://collections.yadvashem.org/en/about/o3128?utm_source=openai))

The USHMM further notes that the Kielce massacre intensified fear among Poland’s already traumatized Jewish survivors and helped spur their flight from the country. That is a broader consequence, not something the caption alone tells us about the people pictured in Chmielnik. Nor does the supplied evidence show whether any of the nine survivors named in the photograph were present in Kielce, knew the victims, or left Poland after the pogrom. Those connections remain possible avenues for research, not facts to state. ([encyclopedia.ushmm.org](https://encyclopedia.ushmm.org/content/en/article/the-kielce-pogrom-a-blood-libel-massacre-of-holocaust-survivors))

The available independent sources therefore add substantial context about the Kielce massacre and postwar anti-Jewish violence, but they do not corroborate the survivors’ caption or independently identify these four Chmielnik victims. The memorial book’s evidence remains essential—and specific in its grief—but its variant spellings and incomplete naming should remain visible. Establishing whether “Shmuel Weinberg,” “Shmuel Weigberg,” and “Shmuel Veinberg” refer to one person, and identifying “Frau Flutga” more fully, are worthwhile next questions. So is learning what became of the survivors in the 1945 photograph, including [Rebeka Sametband] and the Wigadni family. The surviving caption offers a beginning: a named group in Chmielnik, one year before four people from the town were remembered among those killed in Kielce.
